cards.q: What are the five canonical design attributes a network should satisfy?
cards.a: Fault tolerance, scalability, QoS, and security (the Cisco four characteristics of network design), plus manageability and automation as the modern fifth pillar.

cards.q: How does ENCOR typically test network design principles?
cards.a: By presenting a design scenario and asking which principle it satisfies or violates.

cards.q: What does fault tolerance require beyond simply having two devices?
cards.a: It requires eliminating single points of failure with redundant links and devices plus rapid convergence (RSTP/EtherChannel, HSRP/VRRP, NSF/SSO). Designed tolerance means some failures are detected and recovered faster than others, not just 'two of everything'.

cards.q: What does scalability mean in network design?
cards.a: A hierarchical design so adding more sites or users does not require redesigning the core; modular blocks grow vertically (DC) or horizontally (campus), and the address plan has room to grow using VLSM and summarization.

cards.q: What is the purpose of QoS in network design?
cards.a: To differentiate traffic by classifying, marking, and queuing so that traffic such as voice and video is handled first, achieving predictable delay, jitter, and loss under congestion.
Layered controls including ACLs, segmentation (VLAN/VRF/SGT), 802.1X, device hardening, encrypted management, and firewalls, applied as secure-by-design rather than a bolt-on.

cards.q: What does the manageability and automation pillar include?
cards.a: Centralized control (DNA Center/ISE), model-driven APIs (NETCONF/RESTCONF), telemetry, and consistent baselines, which reduce human error and speed change.

cards.q: What are the supporting design rules of hierarchy, modularity, and redundancy?
cards.a: Hierarchy gives consistent behavior and isolation via three-tier or layered modules; modularity keeps functions in blocks so one block can change without touching the rest; redundancy with simplicity means dual everything while avoiding over-engineering such as STP complexities.

cards.q: What do the 80/20 and 20/80 rules describe?
cards.a: The 80/20 rule says local traffic dominates where applications are local, whereas the 20/80 rule applies when most traffic crosses to the core or data center with centralized apps and data. This determines where switches and VLANs are placed.

cards.q: Why does speed of convergence matter more than speed of reconfiguration?
cards.a: For most outages, how quickly the network recovers (speed of convergence) matters more than how fast a configuration change can be made.

cards.q: Which design anti-pattern causes loops or broadcast storms?
cards.a: Redundant links without EtherChannel or STP tuning, which leads to loops and broadcast storms.

cards.q: What happens if a redundant switch pair has a single default gateway?
cards.a: There is no first-hop redundancy, so HSRP or VRRP is missing and a single gateway becomes a failure point.

cards.q: Is having 'two identical switches' enough for redundancy?
cards.a: No. The control plane must also converge, using HSRP/VRRP for gateways, RSTP for loops, and NSF/SSO for supervisor failover.

cards.q: Is QoS about making the internet faster?
cards.a: No. QoS does not increase bandwidth; it reorders and prioritizes existing capacity so important traffic is handled first under congestion.

cards.q: Is one ACL on the edge sufficient for secure design?
cards.a: No. Security is defense-in-depth; a single edge ACL is not 'secure design'. Layered controls, segmented zones, hardened devices, and encrypted management are all required.

cards.q: How should the management plane be protected?
cards.a: The management plane should be placed on a dedicated, separate management segment, ideally a management VRF, so it is not exposed to users.

cards.q: Match the design principle to its exam signal: which uses hybrid convergence, hierarchy, queuing, and segmentation?
cards.a: Fault tolerance signals dual devices plus HA protocols; scalability signals hierarchy with modular design and summarization; QoS signals classification and queuing with voice first; security signals segmentation, 802.1X, hardening, and encrypted management.

cards.q: How does an administrator apply QoS priority to VoIP at the policy level?
cards.a: Create a class-map matching DSCP EF for voice, then in a policy-map assign that class a strict priority queue, for example priority percent 10.

cards.q: What command combines two links into an active EtherChannel?
cards.a: On the port-channel interface, channel-group 1 mode active, which uses LACP and doubles bandwidth while adding high availability.
